summary: Specifies multicast extensions to the CLNP protocol, similar to the ones RFC 1112 gives to IP. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: How to send one message to a group of receivers on an old network type.

questions: how do you join a multicast group on clnp
subtitle: Extensions to send one message to groups of receivers on OSI networks using CLNP.

tldr.problem: CLNP (the OSI network protocol) can only send packets to individual hosts, but applications need to send one message to a group of receivers, similar to IP multicast.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1768 defines group network addresses (special addresses that identify a set of hosts), extensions to the CLNP protocol to recognize and forward multicast packets, and extensions to ES-IS (the routing protocol) to let hosts announce which groups they want to join.
tldr.outcome: Hosts running CLNP can now join multicast groups, send and receive multicast packets, with scope control to limit how far messages travel.

today: RFC 1768 is an Experimental protocol. It was developed during the TUBA (TCP/UDP over Bigger Addresses) working group's exploration of CLNP-based internets in the early 1990s. This specification did not become a standard; the IETF adopted IPv6 instead of pursuing CLNP-based approaches. OSI protocols have largely been superseded by IP-based networking.

sections.title: CLNP Multicasting Basics
sections.content:
RFC 1768 adds multicast capability to CLNP (Connectionless Network Protocol, defined in ISO 8473), the OSI equivalent of the Internet Protocol. It mirrors the multicast extensions that RFC 1112 added to IP.

In CLNP multicast, a host group is a set of zero or more End Systems (hosts) identified by a single group network address. A multicast datagram sent to a group address is delivered to all members of that group with the same best-effort reliability as ordinary unicast packets: arrival is not guaranteed, and packets may arrive out of order or be duplicated.

Host group membership is dynamic: End Systems can join and leave groups at any time. A host may be a member of multiple groups simultaneously. Membership is not restricted by location or number. An End System need not be a member of a group to send datagrams to it. A group may be permanent (with an administratively assigned address) or transient (created dynamically).
sections.plainLanguage: CLNP is the OSI network protocol. Multicast lets you send one packet to a whole group of computers instead of just one. Any computer can send to a group, even if it isn't in the group. Computers can join and leave groups whenever they want.

sections.title: Group Network Addresses
sections.content:
A group network address is a new type of CLNP address that identifies a multicast group, distinct from the individual Network Service Access Points (NSAPs) used for unicast addressing. The RFC allocates 90 new Authority and Format Identifier (AFI) values (in the first octet of the address) reserved exclusively for group addresses, each paired with a corresponding unicast AFI value.

The syntax of a group network address is identical to an individual address except for the AFI value: individual and group address blocks allocated by an addressing authority are differentiated only by their AFI values. This approach leaves existing address families unchanged and does not require new addressing authorities.

Group network addresses may only appear in the destination address field of a CLNP packet; the source address must always be an individual network address. This restriction prevents multicast loops and confusing response routing.

The Domain Specific Part (DSP) of a group address—the portion after the AFI—is assigned by the addressing authority and is outside the scope of this specification, allowing flexibility in how groups are organized and named.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast addresses are new types of CLNP addresses. They look like regular addresses but start with special numbers that mark them as groups. You can't use a group address as the sender's address, only as the destination.

sections.title: CLNP Protocol Extensions
sections.content:
CLNP itself needed modifications to support multicast. A new packet type, the Multicast Data (MD) PDU, was created with type code 11101 (binary), distinct from ordinary Data (DT) PDUs. This marking is critical: non-multicast-capable routers that encounter an unknown packet type must discard it, preventing unpredictable forwarding behavior.

The protocol defines how multicast-capable routers identify and forward multicast packets. The header format analysis function checks that source addresses are never group addresses and discards violating packets. The route PDU function determines which networks to forward a multicast packet to, potentially creating multiple copies. The forward PDU function sends the copies.

Multicast packets do not support source routing; the NS provider must reject any multicast PDU with source route parameters. Error reporting is carefully controlled: a multicast PDU may not cause the origination of another multicast PDU, and packets with group source addresses must not generate error reports, preventing broadcast storms and response floods.

MD and DT PDUs may contain the same optional parameters except that source routing is permitted in DT PDUs but not MD PDUs, while scope control is permitted only in MD PDUs.
sections.plainLanguage: CLNP packets are marked with a special type code so routers know they're multicast. Routers make copies and send them to multiple networks. Error messages are turned off for multicast to prevent the network from being flooded with responses.

sections.title: Scope Control
sections.content:
The scope control function allows the originator of a multicast packet to limit how far it travels. Two forms of scope control exist.

Prefix-based scope control uses address prefixes to restrict forwarding. The originator specifies a set of address prefixes; routers forward the packet only if one of the prefixes matches the beginning of the router's Network Entity Title (NET). This allows multicast to be confined to networks within a particular administrative domain or hierarchy.

Radius scope control limits the logical distance packets travel. Each router that handles a multicast packet with a radius parameter decrements the radius field by an administratively set amount (between 0 and the maximum field value). When the radius reaches 0, the packet is no longer forwarded. This creates a hop-count-like mechanism, though configurable per domain: intra-domain routers might decrement by one; inter-domain routers might decrement to zero (blocking inter-domain multicast) or to a larger value if a policy agreement exists.

When both forms are applied to the same packet, forwarding ceases once either limit is reached. Neither form triggers error reporting, so discarded packets do not generate responses.
sections.plainLanguage: Scope control stops a multicast packet from traveling too far. One way uses address prefixes to say "only send to routers in this domain." Another way uses a hop counter that decrements as the packet travels, eventually reaching 0 and stopping.

sections.title: ES-IS Protocol Extensions for Multicast
sections.content:
The ES-IS protocol (End System to Intermediate System routing protocol, ISO 9542) was extended to let hosts announce which multicast groups they belong to and to let routers map group addresses to data-link addresses.

Hosts use End System Group Hello (ESGH) PDUs to announce the multicast groups they wish to receive. An End System periodically originates ESGH PDUs on each subnetwork where it wants to receive multicast traffic, identifying the group network addresses and their associated data-link addresses (such as IEEE 802 MAC addresses). Multiple groups may be announced in a single ESGH PDU, provided they are for the same subnetwork and holding time.

Multicast Address Mapping (MAM) PDUs are originated by the Active Multicast Intermediate System on each subnetwork to inform End Systems which data-link address to use for each group. When a multicast IS receives an ESGH with an incorrect mapping, or receives a multicast packet using the wrong data-link address, it sends MAM PDUs with corrected information. Without pre-configured mappings, End Systems default to sending to an all-multicast-capable-systems data-link address.

End Systems may optionally perform damping—suppressing their own announcements—if they observe another End System announcing the same group with the same data-link address on the same subnetwork. This reduces announcement traffic during stable periods.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need to know which groups each computer belongs to. Computers send special hello messages saying "I want to receive group X." Routers then send back messages saying "send your group X traffic to this data-link address." This way all the computers in the group can receive the multicast packets.

sections.title: Conformance Levels
sections.content:
RFC 1768 defines three levels of conformance to support gradual deployment:

Level 0 provides no multicast support. Level 0 hosts and routers are unaffected by multicast activity and quietly discard multicast PDUs (which use reserved packet types and group addresses).

Level 1 supports sending multicast PDUs but not receiving them. A Level 1 End System must know whether a multicast-capable router exists on its subnetwork to determine the correct data-link destination address. Level 1 hosts implement all parts of the specification except multicast announcement (ESGH). While it is possible for a Level 1 host to originate multicast PDUs without multicast address mapping information by using the all-multicast-capable-systems address, this is inefficient and should be avoided when a host continues to originate multicast for the same group.

Level 2 provides full multicast support: the ability to join and leave multicast groups and both send and receive multicast PDUs. This requires implementation of all parts of the specification, including multicast announcement and address mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three levels: Level 0 does nothing with multicast, just ignores it. Level 1 can send multicast but not receive or join groups. Level 2 can do everything: join groups, send, and receive.
